caveat: Outlook is an analytical assessment as of October 2026, not a forecast. 2025 figures are IMF estimates/projections.
data_source: IMF World Economic Outlook via DataMapper (latest vintage, accessed October 2026)
debt_management: Lithuania's debt rose from 17.3% of GDP in 2006 (14.6% in 2008, the low) to 45.9% in 2020, the series peak, on COVID spending — the largest increase of the three Baltic states. It fell to 38.3% in 2022 and is projected at 39.8% in 2025. GDP grew from $30.1bn in 2006 to a projected $94.9bn in 2025. Euro adoption in January 2015 cut borrowing costs; defense spending since 2022 has kept deficits higher than the pre-pandemic norm. Debt remains moderate and sustainable.
inflation_management: Lithuania's inflation mirrors Latvia's: 11.1% in 2008 on the credit boom, -0.7% in 2015 (the low), 1.1% in 2020, then 18.9% in 2022, the series high — among the eurozone's highest on energy dependence. It fell to 0.9% in 2024, one of the fastest disinflations in the area, and is projected at 3.4% for 2025. ECB policy is the instrument since the 2015 euro adoption; the domestic pattern is rapid pass-through both ways, reflecting the flexible, small, open economy.

key_events.event: Boom-bust and internal devaluation defended the euro peg through the financial crisis.
Joined the euro area (January 2015), the last Baltic state to adopt the euro.
COVID-19: debt hit 45.9% of GDP, the series peak, on pandemic spending.
Energy shock: inflation hit 18.9%; Lithuania was the first EU country to halt Russian gas imports.
Defense spending rose sharply; debt projected at 39.8% of GDP.

outlook_next_decade: Lithuania's outlook combines sound macroeconomics with elevated geopolitics: euro membership, moderate debt, and fast-adjusting markets are strengths, while the security environment keeps defense spending high and investment risk premia elevated. Inflation should stay near target as energy diversification (the LNG terminal and interconnectors) reduces the 2022-type vulnerability. The base case is solid convergence growth; demographics and the regional security situation are the main structural drags.
